title: Longest Consecutive Run
statement: Given an unsorted list of integers, return the length of the longest run of consecutive values (like 4, 5, 6, 7) that all appear in the list. The values can be anywhere in the list, and duplicates count once.

tests.purpose: catches walking every run from every value

optimal.approach_name: hash set, counting only from the start of each run

acceptable_suboptimal.note: Sorting, then scanning while skipping duplicates, is a good answer too.

hint_ladder.hint: How could you check whether a value's neighbour is in the list without scanning the whole list?
A set gives O(1) membership checks, which is exactly what this needs.
Put everything in a set. A value starts a run only if value - 1 is missing; from each start, count upward while the next value exists. Each run is walked once, so the total is O(n).
values = set(nums). For each v where v - 1 is not in values: length = 1; while v + length in values: length += 1; keep the best length.

common_mistakes.description: Counting upward from every value instead of only from run starts. The answers are right, but it is O(n^2) on one long run.
Sorting first, then letting a duplicate value break the run.
Taking max() of an empty list, which crashes on empty input.
